exam: What radiographic measurements determine instability — list the thresholds and explain why they matter — answer: dorsal angulation >10°, radial shortening >2 mm, volar tilt loss >10°, intra‑articular step >2 mm; these predict loss of reduction.

A 70‑year‑old woman presents with a distal radius fracture and osteoporosis. Would you choose casting or surgery and why — answer: casting is first line if fracture is stable; surgery reserved for unstable patterns or functional demands.

Describe the step‑by‑step closed reduction technique for a dorsally displaced fracture — answer: longitudinal traction, dorsal pressure on the fragment, volar pressure on the distal fragment, wrist flexion, confirm alignment clinically and radiographically.

What are the red‑flag signs of compartment syndrome in the forearm after a distal radius fracture — answer: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, pulselessness; requires urgent fasciotomy.

How does an open distal radius fracture change your management — answer: give IV antibiotics (cover gram‑positive and gram‑negative), tetanus update, surgical debridement, and consider external fixation if soft‑tissue coverage is limited.
Explain why NSAIDs should be avoided in a patient with a suspected infection — answer: they may mask fever and impair platelet function, increasing bleeding risk during surgery.
What physiotherapy measures are started after cast removal — answer: gentle wrist flexion/extension, grip strengthening, and range‑of‑motion exercises to prevent stiffness.

How would you manage a distal radius fracture in a patient with severe malaria‑related thrombocytopenia — answer: prioritize closed reduction and casting; delay surgery until platelet count improves, use blood products if needed.
ai.title: Distal Radius Fracture
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A distal radius fracture is a break near the wrist end of the radius, often from a fall. Management depends on displacement, patient age, and resources. Early recognition and appropriate fixation prevent deformity and functional loss.

b: Mechanism: fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) – dorsal displacement (Colles) or volar displacement (Smith).
Typical presentation: wrist pain, swelling, deformity, limited motion.
sections.p: A fracture of the distal radius occurs within 2 cm of the radiocarpal joint. It is the most common upper‑extremity fracture, especially in older women with osteoporosis and in young men after high‑energy trauma.

b: Extra‑articular fractures are usually stable if <10 mm dorsal angulation and <2 mm radial shortening.
Articular step‑off >2 mm or volar tilt loss >10° often needs operative reduction.
sections.p: Assess displacement, articular involvement, and neurovascular status. Classify using the AO/OTA system (type A – extra‑articular, B – partial articular, C – complete articular) and the Frykman classification for teaching.

b: Check median nerve (sensory loss in thumb, index, middle fingers) and radial artery pulse.
Identify open fractures – risk of infection, especially with contaminated wounds.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, delayed or inadequate treatment leads to malunion, loss of grip strength, and median nerve compression. Early reduction and proper immobilisation are essential.

t.b: Confirms fracture pattern, displacement, and joint involvement; guides need for reduction.
Detects compartment syndrome or nerve injury; if abnormal, urgent surgical review.

t.b: Ensures alignment is maintained; if worsening, arrange transfer for imaging.

b: Closed reduction technique: longitudinal traction, dorsal/volar pressure, and wrist flexion/extension as needed.
Immobilise in a sugar‑tong splint or above‑elbow cast for 4–6 weeks.
Avoid NSAIDs in patients with active infection or renal disease; prefer paracetamol or opioids short‑term.
sections.p: Initial: analgesia, splint, and prompt closed reduction if displaced. Definitive: cast immobilisation for stable fractures; percutaneous K‑wire or volar locking plate for unstable or intra‑articular fractures.

b: Assuming all distal radius fractures are extra‑articular – always check the joint line.
Relying solely on pain relief to judge reduction success – confirm with repeat X‑ray.
sections.p: Typical errors include missing median nerve injury, under‑estimating displacement, and using inadequate immobilisation.

whenToSeekHelp: Increasing pain despite analgesia, progressive swelling, or loss of pulse – possible compartment syndrome.
New sensory loss in the median nerve distribution.
Open wound with contamination or gross deformity.
